---
title: "Overview"
subtitle: "Why replacing a hospital sink didn't fix the resistance problem — and the workflow that revealed it."
---

Replace a contaminated hospital sink and you'd expect the antibiotic-resistance
problem to go down the drain. It didn't.

When **[Kotay et al. (2025, *npj Antimicrobials & Resistance*)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44259-025-00176-2)**
ripped out and replaced the sink plumbing in six ICU rooms, the gleaming new
drains were recolonised within weeks — and came back carrying *more* antibiotic
resistance genes than the old ones, including mobile, clinically feared
carbapenemases. The reservoir didn't reset. It rebooted, worse.

How do you spot a surge like that in a soup of metagenomic reads? With the same
two-tool workflow the study leaned on — and that's exactly what you'll run here.

## What you'll do

Three short steps, start to finish:

1. **[VANISH](https://github.com/hsgweon/vanish)** — quality-control the reads and make the human DNA *vanish*.
2. **[ResScan](https://github.com/hsgweon/resscan)** — quantify the AMR genes that remain, normalised *per bacterial cell*.
3. **Analysis** — watch the resistome climb after the sinks were swapped.

## What you'll run it on

A **bite-size slice** of the real study: the first **10,000 read pairs** from each
of the 36 sink samples. Small enough to download in seconds and run on a laptop —
enough to *see every step work for real*.

::: {.callout-note}
## Ten thousand reads is a keyhole view
Too shallow for meaningful biology, but perfect for learning the mechanics. So the
final **analysis** step uses the **full-depth results** (provided) — that's where the
science actually shows up. The complete raw data lives on NCBI SRA under BioProject
**[PRJNA587635](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA587635)**.
:::
